title: Mean-Field Control on Sparse Graphs: From Local Limits to GNNs via Neighborhood Distributions
claim: A large finite network system reduces to a limiting distribution over local neighborhoods, and optimal decisions need only a horizon-shrinking neighborhood radius.
layout: 3 regions: top-left to top-right graph limit, bottom time axis with shrinking radii
description: The figure has two parts. The top row shows a finite sparse network on the left. It sits in a light blue disc with white circular nodes, and a central red node i is the agent. A thick grey arrow labeled 'N → ∞, Local Weak Limit' leads to a grey disc on the right. That disc holds a rooted tree with a red root ρ and the label μ_t. Bold captions name the Finite System and the Sparse MF Limit, and a System State annotation reads μ_t ∈ P(G*^X), a distribution over decorated rooted graphs. The bottom half is a time axis from t=0 to t=T. Blue dots carry dashed circles that shrink from large radius (k=T) to medium (k=T−t) to none (k=0). A brace below links to 'Theorem 2: Horizon-Dependent Locality'. The eye goes first to the graph on the upper left.
caption: Overview of the Sparse Mean-Field Control Framework. (Top Left) The physical $N$-agent system on a sparse graph where agents interact locally. (Top Right) The rigorous mean-field limit where the state is redefined as a probability measure $\boldsymbol{\mu}_t$ over the space of decorated rooted graphs. (Bottom) Our Horizon-Dependent Locality result (Theorem [ref]) establishes the $(T-t)$-hop neighborhood at time $t$ as sufficient statistic for optimal control.
abstract: Mean-field control (MFC) offers a scalable solution to the curse of dimensionality in multi-agent systems but traditionally hinges on the restrictive assumption of exchangeability via dense, all-to-all interactions. In this work, we bridge the gap to real-world network structures by proposing a rigorous framework for MFC on large sparse graphs. We redefine the system state as a probability measure over decorated rooted neighborhoods, effectively capturing local heterogeneity. Our central contribution is a theoretical foundation for scalable reinforcement learning in this setting. We prove horizon-dependent locality: for finite-horizon problems, an agent's optimal policy at time t depends strictly on its (T-t)-hop neighborhood. This result renders the infinite-dimensional control problem tractable and underpins a novel Dynamic Programming Principle (DPP) on the lifted space of neighborhood distributions. Furthermore, we formally and experimentally justify the use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for actor-critic algorithms in this context. Our framework naturally recovers classical MFC as a degenerate case while enabling efficient, theoretically grounded control on complex sparse topologies.
